AnswerDecisionRequest.description:
Body of ``POST /api/hitl/{plan_id}/decisions/{decision_id}/answer``.

``option`` is the answer, ``answered_by`` who gave it and ``note``
the free-form remark that travels with it into the audit mirror.
The option is stored as given: which of the offered options it is
is not this route's business to decide.
AnswerDecisionRequest.title: AnswerDecisionRequest

CapacityRequest.description:
The request body of ``POST /api/scheduler/capacity``.

Two fields, two meanings:

* ``total`` — the capacity the operator asks for: a whole number
  between 1 and 64, or ``None`` to put the configured one back;
* ``reset`` — put the configured capacity back.

``total`` is typed ``Any`` and not ``int`` **on purpose**: a model
that typed it as an integer would quietly turn ``"5"`` into ``5``
and ``true`` into ``1`` before the route ever saw them — and
neither is the number that was asked for.  The model here only
**takes the request in**; whether the number is one the scheduler
may run with is the route's answer to give, and it gives it with a
400 that says what was wrong.

total.description: how many plans may run at the same time; null puts the configured capacity back
total.title: Total

CapacityRequest.title: CapacityRequest

CreateDecisionRequest.description:
Body of ``POST /api/hitl/{plan_id}/decisions``.

``question`` and ``options`` are the two things a decision cannot
be made of: what is being asked, and what the answers on the table
are.  ``default_option`` is the answer to use when nobody replies
in time, and it has to be one of the offered options.

``mode`` and ``timeout_sec`` are the *request's* own defaults.  The
plan's ``hitl_config.json`` decides what is actually stored — a
decision keeps the meaning it was created with even when the plan's
configuration is rewritten afterwards (see
:func:`hitl.service.create_decision`).  They are accepted here
because the service's own rules read them: a request whose own
timeout is not a positive number of seconds is refused rather than
stored.

``vp_id`` / ``failure_class`` / ``round`` say *what the question is
about* — the verification point, the class of the failure that
raised it, and the round of the verification loop it was raised in.
They are what makes a decision findable by the failure it is
about, rather than only by the plan it belongs to.

``answer_note`` is a remark recorded with the question.  A note
that comes with an answer replaces it.
CreateDecisionRequest.title: CreateDecisionRequest

ImportPlanRequest.description:
Body of ``POST /api/plan/import``.

``project_dir`` is required and ``content`` is declared as ``Any`` on
purpose. The imported material is an upstream input the caller owns, so
nothing about its shape is this route's business: a string, a bare
array, an object with keys nobody here has heard of — all three are
accepted and all three are stored verbatim. The three aliases are the
same slot under different names, because which one a caller reaches for
is a habit, not a requirement; exactly one of them must be present.
ImportPlanRequest.title: ImportPlanRequest

ResetRoundsRequest.description:
Operator payload for ``POST /api/verification/{plan_id}/reset_rounds``.

2026-09-16 — the endpoint was renamed from
``reset_max_rounds`` because that name described the *original*
behaviour, not the current one: a name that says "max rounds" tells
the reader this rewrites the budget when it resets the counter.

The rename follows the 2026-09-14 semantic inversion. The decision
behind it: the cap is not what this endpoint is for. The budget is
set when the plan is created and is not meant to move afterwards;
the counter is the part that legitimately needs to be rewound, and
only with the operator's authorization.

So: ``max_rounds`` is the plan's budget and is immutable (raising it
makes rounds unbounded — the 2026-08-25 incident; lowering it
silently rewrites the plan's setup contract). What the operator
actually needs is another *batch*: reset the round counter and the
auto-loop may iterate up to ``max_rounds`` again. "reset_rounds"
says exactly that.
ResetRoundsRequest.title: ResetRoundsRequest

ResetVerificationRequest.description:
Operator payload for ``POST /api/verification/{plan_id}/reset``.

2026-09-17: a manual restart must set the verification state
directly rather than walk the state machine from one point to the
next. Routing it through the transition table is what lets the
machine drift into states nobody asked for, and it makes every
restart depend on the transitions the current stage happens to
allow. A reset is a fixed procedure — "clear what should be
cleared" — so writing the post-reset state outright is both safer
and simpler.

This makes it a HARD RESET, in contrast with
:class:`ResetRoundsRequest`, which is explicitly a *budget* reset —
"verdicts / runtime state survive".

Attributes:
    force: proceed even when a verification thread is live. The
        hard reset is not safe against a running round (that thread
        holds the orchestrator and keeps writing), so it refuses by
        default; ``force`` first signals the round to cancel, then
        resets. Without it a live round answers 409.
    clear_artifacts: delete the per-round disk outputs
        (``verification_report.json``,
        ``verification_execution_results.json``,
        ``verification_repair_tasks.json``,
        ``verification_loop_tracking.json``,
        ``logs/verification_*``, ``screenshots/verification_*``).

        ``verification_plan.json`` is deliberately **not** in this
        list any more — see ``clear_verification_plan``.
    clear_verification_plan: also delete ``verification_plan.json``,
        so the next round re-runs Phase-1 and regenerates the VP list
        from scratch. Off by default.

        2026-09-19: a reset clears the round counter without
        touching the VP list.

        The VP list is the only thing in this reset that the *next*
        generation of the plan is keyed against, and its ids are
        positional (``VP-0NN``). Regenerating recycles those ids onto
        different verification points, so every cross-batch artefact
        keyed by VP id — ``verification_failure_history.json`` above
        all, which is what the repair prompt renders as "上次修复尝试
        未生效" — silently re-attributes the previous batch's verdicts
        to the current batch's same-numbered VPs — a VP list that
        grows from one batch to the next keeps its ``VP-0NN`` ids
        while their meaning changes underneath.

        The reason the file used to be deleted — "leaving a stale
        plan behind is how a reset silently keeps the old verdict
        set" — no longer holds: the verdict set lives in
        ``plan_verification`` (``results`` / ``verdicts`` /
        ``runtime_state`` / ``executor_state`` / ``progress_state``
        / ``execution_results``) and this same reset clears those,
        plus the executor sidecars go on the next round's
        ``_clear_verification_state_files``. Nothing in
        ``verification_plan.json`` is per-round state — its top level
        is ``services`` + ``verification_points``, and every VP field
        is definitional.

        Turn it on when the plan itself was regenerated (PRD revised,
        tasks re-cut) and a fresh VP list is actually what you want.
    clear_root_cause_chain: also delete the root-cause chain's
        ledger (``verification_root_cause_chain.json``) and the
        reports it names (``vps[*].report_path``).

        2026-10-30: the chain outlived every other per-round
        artefact. A reset clears the verdicts, the repair tasks and
        the round's disk outputs, but the ledger stayed — so the
        next round still saw the old ``BLOCKED_ON_USER`` entry and
        the point stayed occupied by a chain nobody had re-examined.
        The report is the other half: the ledger says the diagnosis
        was delivered, and the reader judges that by whether the
        report file is there.

        Off by default: clearing the chain is a **decision** (the
        chain is the plan's own history of where each point's root
        cause stood), not a side effect of a reset. When it is on,
        only the files the ledger names are deleted — the reports
        directory is never globbed.
    supersede_repair_tasks: mark pending ``RP-*`` tasks
        ``superseded``. They were generated from the verdicts this
        reset is discarding, so leaving them pending would have the
        executor run repairs for failures that no longer exist.
        Nothing is ever deleted — see the task-data rule.
    restart_at_round: the 1-based round the next ``/start`` begins
        at (same numbering the card shows). Default 1 = the full
        batch. May not exceed the plan's immutable ``max_rounds``.
ResetVerificationRequest.title: ResetVerificationRequest

RevisePlanRequest.description:
Body of ``POST /api/plan/{plan_id}/revise``.

``feedback`` is the caller's note about the task list as a whole —
the reason this door exists. It is required and must not be empty:
a revision with nothing to say is not a revision, and treating it as
one would ask the model to redo the list for no reason and charge
the caller for the answer.

``content`` optionally replaces the imported material, so a caller
who also has new upstream material hands it over in the same round
trip. It is stored verbatim, exactly as the import stores its own.
RevisePlanRequest.title: RevisePlanRequest

StartInterviewRequest.description:
``POST /api/interview/start``'s body, plus the plan's hook binding.

The two extra fields say which session created the plan and where a
human-in-the-loop question about it should be delivered.  Both are
optional and mean exactly what they mean on ``POST /api/plan/import``:
a plan started without them asks nobody, which is the right answer
for a plan started by a bare ``curl`` rather than a failure.

``hook_destination`` is the cc-connect project the question is
delivered to and ``hook_session_id`` is the cc-connect session key
inside it.  They are the two arguments of the delivery command: the
hook this origin implies is a ``cmd`` hook whose command runs
``backend.hooks.session_send`` with those two values, and that
module is what actually delivers the message.  The protocol is the
same as the fast lane's — same field names, same types, same
defaults.
StartInterviewRequest.title: StartInterviewRequest

StartPlanRequest.description:
``POST /api/plan/{plan_id}/lifecycle/start`` 的请求体。

五个字段**全部可选**，缺什么由被派发的那一侧按它自己的规矩补：

* ``project_dir`` —— 执行侧的工作目录。**全新执行必须带**（没有检查点
  时它没有别处可取）。
* ``tool`` —— 编码工具。
* ``max_rounds`` —— 验证轮次预算（只对验证侧有意义）。
* ``sync_targets`` —— 下游通知落点（只对执行侧有意义）。取值是闭集，
  写错的那个在**这里**就被拒（422），不会等到派发出去才炸。
* ``force`` —— 验证侧「已有报告也重跑」（只对验证侧有意义）。
StartPlanRequest.title: StartPlanRequest

StopPlanRequest.description:
``POST /api/plan/{plan_id}/lifecycle/stop`` 的请求体。

``requeue`` —— 停完之后是否把计划迁回等待相位 ``queued``。默认 ``False``
（停下就停着，不塞回队列）。
StopPlanRequest.title: StopPlanRequest

TaskDeltaRequest.description:
Operator payload for ``POST /api/execution/{plan_id}/task_delta``.

Two actions, matching the verification side's
``verification_plan_delta`` contract (see ``backend/task_plan_delta.py``):

  * ``add``     — new task; must carry ``title``, ``reason`` and
                   ``test_command``.
  * ``obsolete`` — mark an existing task void (``id`` + ``reason``).
                   Marked, never deleted, and the task's own fields
                   are not touched.

Attempting to *modify* an existing task (reusing its id in ``add``)
is rejected and recorded in ``rejected_modifications`` rather than
applied.
TaskDeltaRequest.title: TaskDeltaRequest

_ExecutionStatusResponse.description:
The status answer, plus the provenance of that answer.

``data_source`` says where the answer came from: ``state_db`` when
it was assembled from the durable ``plan_execution`` row, and
``default`` when the library really holds no row for this plan and
the answer is the empty default.

The field exists because the two answers used to look alike.  A
reader that got ``status=not_started`` with every other field null
could not tell "this plan never ran" from "this process knows
nothing about this plan" — and the second one is what a run that
was dying looked like.

``data_source_detail`` is the same provenance in facts rather than
in a word: the database by path and by inode, the moment the read
opened it, the row it found (by rowid and by the row's own stamp)
and the verdict of the integrity check that ran before the row was
trusted.  The kind alone is not enough inside a round that restarts
the service: two instances can read two different snapshots of the
same file, and a reader that cannot tell the snapshots apart
cannot tell which run it is being told about.

Declared as a subclass of the server's own model rather than as an
edit to it: the server module owns the shared response models, and
a route-local subclass inherits every field it already had — the
status vocabulary, the pause fields — without a second place to
keep them in sync.
_ExecutionStatusResponse.title: _ExecutionStatusResponse

_VerificationPlanReviewActionRequest.description:
计划书审核动作的请求体。

Attributes:
    action: ``accept`` / ``skip`` / ``reset`` / ``revise``。
    note: 原因。``skip`` 必须给非空原因；``revise`` 的 note 是 refine 反馈。
    doc_sha256: **可选**：审核者读到的那一版文档的字节哈希。不带它时，
        端点只能拿已落盘的审核状态去比「文档是不是被改过」。
_VerificationPlanReviewActionRequest.title: _VerificationPlanReviewActionRequest

get.description: Get architecture design.

post.description: Append a new CPEA decision point to arch-design.md.
Generate architecture design from approved PRD.
Refine architecture based on rejected review items or direct feedback.
Regenerate architecture design — clears existing arch and review data.
Submit architecture review action.

get.description: Get architecture review items.

AI-friendly diagnostic summary for stuck or failed executions.

Analyzes execution logs to detect patterns: repeated failures, timeouts,
refinement loops, stuck duration, etc. Returns actionable suggestions.

List files currently in the project directory (excludes vcs/build dirs).

Useful for AI agents to understand the realized system architecture.

The recursive scan is cached per ``project_dir`` for
``_FILES_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS`` (see :data:`_FILES_CACHE`) so repeated
polls within the TTL do not re-walk the tree. The 404 path is
checked before the cache read, so a missing project directory is
never served from a stale entry.

Query structured execution logs with filters.

The answer says WHICH tree it read.  A 404 that names only "Plan
not found" is the same answer for a plan this process does not
have and for a plan that is in another instance's plans root, and
the two must not look alike: the first is a fact about the plan,
the second is a fact about the probe.  So the 404 carries the root
it searched and the directory it resolved, and the 200 carries the
file it actually read — which is what lets a reader confirm after
a round that the evidence came from that round's instance.

Args:
    level: Minimum log level (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL)
    task_id: Filter by task ID
    event: Filter by event type (e.g., task_failed, refine_completed)
    limit: Maximum entries to return (default 100, max 1000)
    since: ISO timestamp — return entries after this time

Real-time task progress.

Resolution order (architecture decision point 3):

  1. ``plan_execution.task_progress`` (SQLite) — the
     ``ExecutionRepository.progress()`` snapshot is the
     authoritative counts when present.
  2. ``<PLANS_DIR>/<plan_id>/tasks.json`` — legacy fallback for
     plans that haven't yet been migrated to the state-machine
     task_progress write path.  ``cli.py --recover`` writes here
     (via ``--tasks-file``), so we still consult it to derive
     counts when the SQLite column is empty.
  3. ``<project_dir>/tasks.json`` — pre-refactor fallback.

The ``current`` / ``next`` / ``api_error`` fields are still
derived from the on-disk tasks.json (the per-task rich
metadata that ``task_progress`` does not carry).  The
``pid`` / ``project_dir`` / ``execution_status`` fields are
derived from the state-machine row + on-disk ``execution.json``
mirror, NOT from ``_execution_state`` (no in-memory aggregation).

2026-10-24 — the 404 gate is "there is no execution record", not
"there is no project dir".  The gate used to read
``_get_project_dir()`` and answer 404 when it came back empty,
which reported a quota-parked plan as a plan that was never
started: the parked row exists, but nothing forces that row to
carry a project directory, so the operator's question ("what is
still left to do?") was answered with "call /start first" — on a
plan that was already running and waiting for capacity.

The ``plan_execution`` row IS the evidence that the plan was
configured for execution.  Only its ABSENCE may produce the 404,
and the original wording stays for that case: an operator who
reads "not configured" can act on it.

2026-10-26 — **the row is the truth and the registry is a cache.**
The row (``plan_execution``) is the durable record of the run and
the per-task rows (``plan_tasks``) are the durable record of the
work; the in-memory registry (``_execution_state``) is one
process's view of the row, and it goes stale the moment another
process touches the plan.  A plan parked on capacity by the process
that owns the run leaves every OTHER process holding a registry
that still says "running" — with a pid that has since exited.

The watchdog (``_lazy_check_execution``) judges the registry's
status and probes the registry's pid, so a stale "running" made it
judge a parked plan's dead pid: the pause was rewritten as a crash,
the row was overwritten with ``failed``, and the interrupted task's
``in_progress`` row was reaped back to ``pending``.  The plan then
reported "nothing is running and two tasks are still pending" for
work that was merely waiting for capacity.

So the row's verdict is adopted into the registry BEFORE the
watchdog runs, the counts are read from the state database this
process is bound to, and the answer names the instance that
produced it (``serving_instance``) and whether the run is still in
flight (``execution_in_flight``).  A reader can then tell this
answer from another instance's answer about the same plan, and can
tell a paused run from a dead one.

post.description:
Start autonomous task execution as a background subprocess.

Single-instance contract (architecture decision point 4):

  0. Before anything is spawned, the ledger is asked whether this
     plan already has a live executor.  The in-memory handle
     cannot answer that question after a backend restart, and a
     plan with two executors has two runs writing the same task
     rows.  A plan that already has one is refused with HTTP 409
     ``{"error": "already_running", "pids": [...]}``.
     ``?force=true`` sweeps the plan's tree from the ledger first
     and continues only if that sweep was clean; a sweep that left
     something alive answers HTTP 409
     ``{"error": "kill_incomplete", "pids": [...]}``.  Neither
     refusal spawns anything, and neither moves the plan's phase.

State-machine contract (architecture decision point 3):

  1. Reject archived plans with HTTP 410.
  2. CAS ``RoutingRepository.try_mark_phase(pid,
     _EXECUTION_START_SOURCE_PHASES, 'executing')`` — the
     only legitimate states from which ``start`` may succeed.
     A concurrent second ``start`` (or a state we don't expect
     to start from) raises :class:`ConflictError` which we
     surface as HTTP 409.
  3. Persist ``project_dir`` and ``exec_pid`` via
     :meth:`ExecutionRepository.update_fields`.  The workflow
     phase is *not* written here — step 2's routing CAS owns it
     (schema v6: one phase column, one owner).  The transition is
     wrapped in the repository's own
     ``BEGIN IMMEDIATE`` transaction so partial writes are
     impossible.

Resume contract (architecture decision point 4):

  4. A plan that was *stopped* has a pause checkpoint on disk. The
     start continues it: the checkpoint carries the project
     directory the work was happening in (so the operator does not
     have to repeat it, and the request body cannot redirect it),
     and it says per task whether that task continues in its own
     session or is re-run whole. Only the tasks that continue in a
     session are handed to the executor, through
     ``PDT_RESUME_SESSIONS``. A resumed start answers with
     ``resumed`` / ``resume_strategy`` / ``resume_plan`` on top of
     the four fields every start answers with; a fresh start keeps
     the response it has always published. The checkpoint is
     retired only once the executor has been spawned.

get.description:
Poll execution status and logs.

Reads flow through the in-memory ``_execution_state`` dict (which
is restored on startup by :func:`_recover_execution_states` from
the ExecutionRepository SQLite row).  The legacy direct read of
``execution.json`` was removed because writes already flow through
the repository layer — there is no canonical on-disk JSON to
read from at this point.

**The row is the source of the answer; the in-memory map is one
view of it.**  The map lives in the process that started the run, so
it is empty in every process that did not: a fresh boot whose
recovery scan has not run yet, a second process answering for a plan
the first one is running, a plan whose directory the boot-time scan
never walked.  Answering "not started" from an empty map turned a
run that was parked on capacity — or one that was dying — into a
plan that never ran, and the operator was told the run never
happened.  So the row is read first and the answer is made of it:
its ``exec_status``, its ``stop_reason``, its start time, its end
time and its pid.  Only a plan that has no execution row at all is
"not started".

**A row with nothing in the map is restored into it.**  The map is
also what the liveness rule reads — the watchdog judges the
in-memory status and probes the in-memory pid — so a row that says
``running`` while its process is gone would never be probed at all
when the map is empty, and the answer would report a run that is
still going, forever.  Restoring the row (in the very shape the
boot-time scan restores it) hands it to the standing rule instead
of inventing a verdict for it: a process that died is ``failed`` /
``process_died_unexpectedly``, and never a quota wait.

**The row is also the truth when the map holds something.**  The
map is one process's view of a run, and it goes stale the moment
another process touches the same plan — another process parks the
plan on capacity, another process judges a crash.  So the row's
verdict is read first and adopted into the map, and the answer is
made of the row.  That is also what keeps the watchdog honest: it
judges liveness from the in-memory status, and it must not judge a
row that is not ``running``.

**The answer says where it came from.**  ``data_source`` is
``state_db`` when the answer was assembled from the row and
``default`` when the library really holds no row and the answer is
the empty default.  Without it, "this plan never ran" and "this
process knows nothing about this plan" are the same answer — and
the second one is what a dying run used to look like.

**The answer says WHICH database produced it.**  ``data_source``
names the *kind*; ``data_source_detail`` names the *store*: the
database by path and by inode, the moment the read opened it, the
row it found (by rowid and by the row's own stamp) and the verdict
of the integrity check that ran before the row was trusted.  A
round that restarts the service inside the round is exactly where
the kind is not enough: two instances can read two different
snapshots of the same file, and a reader that cannot tell them
apart cannot tell which run it is being told about.

**"Not started" is a claim, and a claim needs a witness.**  The
empty answer is only made when this instance can back it up: the
library was read and it holds no run for this plan.  When the
library could not be read, or when it was read, it holds rows of
its own, and it holds no row at all for a plan whose directory is
right here in this instance's tree, the answer is a refusal (503)
that names the database that could not answer — never a default
nobody recorded.  See
:func:`_refusal_when_the_run_cannot_be_confirmed`.

The read itself never probes a PID on its own: a parked run keeps a
PID whose process is gone, and judging liveness belongs to
``_recover_execution_states`` and ``_lazy_check_execution`` — the
two places allowed to ask it.

The pause fields come from the plan directory rather than from
that state, and are filled in on **every** branch: after a
restart, the branch a paused plan lands in is ``not_started``,
which is exactly where the checkpoint has to still be reported.

post.description:
Stop a running execution — and leave a resume point behind.

A stop is a pause (core contract 1 / 2 / 6): the plan keeps
whatever it had achieved, and the next start picks it up instead
of re-running the whole round.

The order of the four steps is the contract, not an implementation
detail:

  1. **Mark** — the in-memory state says ``stopped`` /
     ``pausing`` and ``exec_status`` is persisted, *before*
     anything is killed. The executor's watcher thread and the
     heartbeat watchdog both act on ``status == "running"``, so a
     kill that landed first could let the executor stamp the
     plan ``failed`` — the one outcome a pause must never
     produce.
  2. **Terminate** — the plan's whole tree is swept from the
     ledger (children first, every signal preceded by an identity
     check); the handle's own process group is the fallback for
     whatever the ledger never knew about. Another plan's
     executor is never touched.
  3. **Checkpoint** — the resume point is written *after* the
     termination completed, so it describes the interruption as
     it actually ended.
  4. **Transition** — the plan state moves to ``stopped``.

``?discard=true`` is the escape hatch: the work is thrown away
instead of paused, the checkpoint is removed, and the answer says
``paused: false``.

The answer says ``stopped`` only when the plan's tree is
*confirmed* dead. A stop that could not kill everything answers
``kill_incomplete`` and names the pids that survived — a stop
that kills nothing and says "stopped" is worse than no stop at
all, because the operator stops looking.

Apply an operator task-list delta (``add`` / ``obsolete``).

Why this exists: a failed execution task previously had only two
outcomes — get repaired, or sit on the progress card as a permanent
red entry. Clearing them would hide the problem; this endpoint adds
the ability to **void** a task with a recorded reason and **add** a
replacement, without editing the original.

Semantics live in ``backend/task_plan_delta.py``; this handler owns
the I/O (load current tasks, open the state-machine connection).

``obsolete`` writes ``status="superseded"`` (already terminal for the
dispatcher) plus an ``[obsolete] …`` marker in ``failure_reason`` —
``plan_tasks`` has no dedicated ``obsolete_reason`` column. The
authoritative audit record (actor, round, reasons for both actions,
and everything that was rejected) goes to
``plans/{plan_id}/task_delta_log.json``.

get.description: API-namespaced liveness probe (alias of /health).

The plan's decisions, oldest first, optionally narrowed to one state.

``status`` is the closed set of five decision states; a value
outside it is a 400 rather than an empty list, because a filter
nobody can interpret would silently return the wrong set.

An unknown plan is not an error but an empty list: the question
this answers is "what is outstanding", not "does the plan exist".

schema.title: Response List Hitl Decisions Api Hitl  Plan Id  Decisions Get

post.description:
Ask a human, on behalf of ``plan_id``, and store the question.

The plan's own configuration is read from its directory and the two
fields it owns — the mode and the timeout — are frozen into the
stored decision, so a question that is already open keeps the
meaning it was created with.

A question that could not become a decision that works — an
``auto`` decision with no default answer, a non-positive timeout,
an empty option set — is refused with a 400 and leaves no row
behind.

schema.title: Response Create Hitl Decision Api Hitl  Plan Id  Decisions Post

post.description:
Record a human's answer to one of the plan's decisions.

The answer is scoped to the plan in the path: a decision of another
plan is reported as not found, so a stale card cannot answer
somebody else's question.

The first answer wins.  A decision that is already settled answers
with a 409 and keeps what it had — a second answer is a conflict,
never an overwrite.

An answer is also the signal that the plan may go back to work, so
the route hands the scheduler the engine it is running with
(``app.state.scheduler_engine`` — the same handle the lifespan
hangs the engine on, and ``None`` while the scheduler is not
running).  The service submits the ``resume`` that puts a parked
plan back at the head of the queue; a plan that is still working is
left alone, and a scheduler that is not there is not a reason to
refuse the answer.

post.description:
Transition plan to a target phase with input completeness checks.

VP-005: When transitioning to ``prd_generation`` and ``interview.json``
is empty (or missing required dimensions), the transition is refused:
the response carries ``status="failed"`` (alias ``"blocked"``) plus
``error_code="PRD_INPUT_INCOMPLETE"``, and ``current_phase`` is rolled
back to ``interview``.

Revise an imported plan's whole task list, in place.

The lane's second door. ``POST /api/plan/import`` is the way in;
this is the way to say "not quite" about what came out. The plan
keeps its directory, its phase and its execution state — only the
task list is replaced, and only after the replacement passes the
same audit the import applied. A rejected revision leaves the plan
exactly as it was: the generator's writes are deferred until the
result has been audited and accepted.

Park a plan: stop it, and let it give its slot back.

A working plan is stopped through the lifecycle's existing stop
path, and a waiting one is taken out of the queue and parked.  In
both cases the plan ends up in ``stopped`` and it stops holding
compute.

Move a plan ahead in the queue — and nothing else.

A promotion is a change of order: it evicts nobody and it takes no
slot, so a plan that is already working cannot be promoted — it is
not waiting in the queue, and there is no order to move it in.  That
is a conflict.

Put a stopped plan back at the head of the queue.

A resume is a **wait**, not a take: the plan comes back first, it
waits for a slot, and it interrupts nobody.

Make a plan the next one to run.

A start is the **only** action that may interrupt somebody, and it
does so only when the capacity is full and there is a victim the
rules allow.  With no such victim the plan waits at the head of the
queue and the answer is ``blocked_by_capacity``.

Refuse what the four fixed endpoints cannot answer.

The four actions are **fixed paths**, and nothing outside them runs:
the vocabulary is closed, so an action that is not one of the four
has no command, no plan and no effect — it is refused with a 404
that says exactly that.

This route exists because the four fixed endpoints **cannot match**
every malformed request, and a request that matches no route at all
is answered by the frontend's catch-all — whose answer is a 405
("this method is not allowed here"), a sentence about the *method*
when the real problem is the *URL*.  Two shapes fall through:

* an **empty** plan id — ``/api/plan//scheduler/promote``.  The
  router's ``{plan_id}`` needs at least one character, so the
  segment is simply not there;
* a plan id that carries a **path separator** — a traversal such as
  ``../../etc/passwd``.  The router splits the path on ``/`` before
  the handler ever sees it, so such an id arrives as *several*
  segments and the fixed route stops matching.

Both are refusals, and both are answered here:

* an action **outside** the closed four → 404: there is no such
  endpoint, and nothing is executed;
* an action **inside** it, with a plan id the router could not
  carry → the shared guard's own 400, unchanged.  The guard is
  ``server._plan_dir``, the one place a request-supplied id may
  become a path, and it refuses an empty id and an id with a
  separator alike.

The route is registered **after** the four fixed ones, so a request
that one of them matches is answered by that one: the four fixed
paths stay the only paths that carry out an action.

get.description:
Return the routing row straight from the state-machine SQLite.

This endpoint is the integration-test seam the task brief
pins: it MUST read ``plan_routing`` directly from
``state.db`` and MUST NOT consult the on-disk plan
directory or the ``plan_state.py`` JSON fallback that
``/api/plan/{plan_id}/state`` uses.

Status codes:

  * **200** — a row exists for ``plan_id``; the body carries
    ``plan_id``, ``current_phase`` (may be ``null``) and
    ``completed_phases`` (decoded list, default ``[]``).
  * **404** — no row in ``plan_routing``; body is
    ``{"error": "plan not found in routing table",
    "error_code": "PLAN_NOT_FOUND"}``.
  * **503** — the state-db file does not exist on disk; body
    is ``{"error": "state db unavailable", "error_code":
    "STATE_DB_MISSING"}``.
  * **500** — sqlite3 raised while reading; body is
    ``{"error": "state db read failed", "error_code":
    "SQLITE_ERROR"}``.

The single, consistent view of one plan — everything a card needs.

Prefer this over reassembling a verdict from
``/summary`` + ``/execution/{id}/progress`` + ``/verification/{id}/progress``:
those are three reads at three instants, and re-deriving an answer
from them is how the card and the database came to disagree
(2026-09-23). The three sub-payloads are still here, for the card
*body* — but they are gathered in one server-side pass, so they
describe one moment. The verdict itself is the top-level
``PlanStatus`` fields.

``divergences`` is empty when the stores agree.

The two ways this route can refuse to answer are a contract of their
own, and they are told apart deliberately:

* a **malformed** id is a bad request — ``400``, with the same body
  every other plan-id route answers it with;
* a **legal but unknown** id is a plan that does not exist —
  ``404`` with the detail ``Plan not found``.

And there is a third answer, which is not about the id at all:
a plans tree this instance **cannot search** is answered ``503``,
because in that state "the plan does not exist" is not a fact this
instance is entitled to state.  An empty tree says "not found"
about every id, and a caller that believes it is looking for a
plan that was deleted never learns that the instance is looking in
the wrong place.  See :func:`_plans_dir_unavailable_reason`.

The same reasoning covers the state plane: an instance whose state
database holds no plan of its own cannot say that a plan it does
not hold is missing, so it answers ``503`` there too.  See
:func:`_serving_plane`.

Every one of those answers carries the facts of the **serving**
instance — the tree that was searched, the state database that was
read (by path and by inode), and the plan ids that instance can
see — because an answer that cannot be attributed to an instance
cannot be told apart from the answer of an instance that is
looking at another round's data plane.  That confusion is what
made two earlier rounds read "the plan is gone" out of an answer
that really said "you asked the wrong instance".

The validation is asked for here rather than left to happen on the
way to ``PLANS_DIR / plan_id``.  ``_plan_dir`` does validate, so the
refusal is observable either way — but a route whose contract rests
on a helper it happens to call has no contract at all: the day that
helper is relaxed (and it is a plausible relaxation, because the
codebase already carries ``_is_renderable_plan_id`` for stored ids
that predate the traversal guard), this route would answer ``200``
with ``plan_id: ".."`` and the repository root's contents as if they
were a plan.  Asking for the guard at the entry is what keeps the
refusal a decision of this route instead of a side effect of
another one.

Aggregated plan summary — route wrapper owning the DB handle.

The payload is built by :func:`_get_plan_summary_body`, which
receives an already-open state-machine handle. Splitting them lets
the connection be released in a ``finally`` even though the body
has a single terminal ``return`` deep inside its own branches.
Return a summary of the plan's tasks with lifecycle counts.

Per-plan LLM usage, aggregated from CC Switch's own ledger.

Answers "what did this plan actually cost" — new input / output /
cache-read / cache-creation tokens plus the billed USD, broken down
by ledger source, provider, model, scene, task and day, with a
cross-check against the backend's own first-hand accounting.

Query params
------------
``refresh=true``
    Re-aggregate before answering. Otherwise the persisted
    ``plans/<id>/usage_report.json`` is returned when present, and
    the report is computed on demand when it is not (so the endpoint
    is useful before the first execution finishes).

List all plans.

By default, plans in terminal states (``stopped``, ``completed``,
``failed``, ``verification_loop_stopped``, ``verification_passed``,
``verification_failed``) are filtered out — they are historical
artifacts that no longer need a sidebar entry. Pass
``?include_terminal=true`` to see the full list (e.g. for
audit / cleanup scripts).

``waiting_for_quota`` is NOT one of the terminal phases: a plan
parked for capacity is alive and will resume when the window opens,
so it stays in the sidebar.

The terminal decision reads TWO verdicts, not one: the routing
phase (the workflow's answer) and the persisted execution row (the
run's answer).  A run that failed or was stopped is over whatever
the workflow phase says — see :func:`_plan_is_terminal`.

Provenance
----------
The answer says which tree it read: ``data_source``
(``state_db`` when the phases came from the state database,
``directory`` when the listing degraded to a directory scan) and
``plans_dir`` (the root it read).  Both appear on every row and on
the response headers, so an empty list from a process pointed at
another worktree's plans root cannot be mistaken for "this
instance has no plans".

The ``data_source`` of a row is a BLOCK, not a word: it carries the
kind (``state_db`` / ``directory``) together with the facts about
the data plane the rows came from — the database by path and by
inode, the process that answered (pid + boot id) and how many rows
it found.  The kind is what the response header carries; the block
is what a reader needs to tell this answer apart from another
instance's answer about the same URL.

Refusal
-------
A plans tree and a state database are two halves of one instance's
world.  When the tree holds plans and the database knows NONE of
them, the two halves belong to different instances — and the
listing built from that database is empty, which is exactly what
"this instance has no plans" looks like on the wire.

So the listing refuses in that case: ``503``, with the data plane
that could not answer named in the body.  An empty array is a
coincidence of shape that a reader takes for a fact; a refusal is
an answer about what this instance could and could not read.

Degradation
-----------
The terminal filter needs the phase, and the phase lives in the
state database.  When that database cannot be opened, the listing
degrades to a directory scan: it answers 200 with every plan it can
see and it CANNOT filter the terminal ones.  Such an answer carries
the degradation marker — on every row
(``list_degraded``) and on the response
(``X-PDT-Plans-List-Degraded``) — because "200 + a full list" is
what a reader takes for "the terminal plans were filtered out".
See :data:`LIST_DEGRADED_KEY`.

Reads
-----
* RoutingRepository.list_all(data_dir=PLANS_DIR) — single
  aggregate call returning BOTH new (SQLite) and archived
  (directory-derived) rows. Archived rows carry
  ``archived=True`` and DO NOT carry stage / current_phase
  fields.
* ExecutionRepository.snapshot_for_list(plan_ids) — the execution
  row of every listed plan, read from the state database.  It
  carries the run's own verdict (``exec_status``), which is part of
  the terminal decision, plus the run-state fields
  (``exec_pid`` / ``project_dir`` …); the workflow phase comes from
  the routing row above, not from here (schema v6).  Archived rows
  have no execution rows so they get ``None``.

Architecture decision point 5 forbids an in-memory aggregation
facade: this route composes the two repositories directly
(no intermediate facade object).  Human-readable fields
(``requirement``, ``created_at``, ``steps``) are still derived
from the on-disk JSON files because those fields are slated
for a separate "interview_repository" / "artifact metadata"
task and are out of scope for this refactor.

Caching
-------
The rendered list is cached in :data:`_PLANS_CACHE` for
:data:`_PLANS_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS` seconds, keyed on the
``include_terminal`` query parameter. Mutation endpoints call
:func:`invalidate_plans_cache` to drop the snapshot the moment
they know it is stale; absent explicit invalidation, the TTL
guarantees self-healing within a small bounded delay.

The degradation verdict and the provenance are read off the cached
rows, so a cache hit reports the same verdict and the same tree the
cache miss did.

get.description:
Quick snapshot of how many the workflow tasks are currently running.

Inspects:
  - _execution_state: per-plan execution subprocess status
  - _verification_state: per-plan verification cycle status
  - Heartbeat check on subprocess poll() to detect "running" state
  - pause checkpoints on disk: plans interrupted but not resumed

Returns:
  {
    "execution_running": <int>,
    "verification_running": <int>,
    "total_active": <int>,
    "details": [
      {"plan_id": ..., "type": "execution"|"verification", "status": ..., ...},
      ...
    ],
    "paused_executions": [
      {"plan_id": ..., "kind": ..., "paused_at": ..., "interrupted_task_count": ...},
      ...
    ]
  }

``paused_executions`` is computed BEFORE the empty-state
short-circuit below and returned from every path. The short-circuit
is exactly the state of a freshly-restarted server — which is the
one moment the pause list matters most, since a plan that was
paused before the restart has no in-memory state left to report.
A response that carried the list only on the non-empty path would
answer "nothing is paused" at precisely the moment a resume is
waiting to be found.

post.description:
Resume the batch this stop stopped, in one call.

The second half of a backend restart, and the counterpart of
:func:`stop_all_tasks`.

The targets are the plans named by the batch the global stop
recorded — and only those. A checkpoint left on disk by an earlier,
unrelated stop is not resumed: the restart belongs to the batch,
not to every pause that ever happened.

Within the batch, a plan is resumed from its pause checkpoint on
disk, or — for a verification whose thread a hard kill took away —
from its recovered state. Each is started by the route that owns
its kind.

The execution start is handed an explicitly empty request: the
checkpoint carries the project directory the work was happening in,
and a request that named one would redirect the resumed work to a
directory it was never written for.

One plan's failure is one row. The others are still started.

The batch is consumed: the record is deleted once the resume has
been attempted, whatever the per-plan outcome, so a second
``start_all`` is a no-op instead of a second resume.

The answer carries the batch it acted on (``"batch"``), and
``"detail"`` when there was none to act on.

Stop every plan that is running, in one call.

The first half of a backend restart, and the counterpart of
:func:`start_all_tasks`. The operator asks for one stop instead of
one stop per plan, and the answer says what happened to each of
them.

The list of plans comes from :func:`get_active_tasks` — the same
read the supervisor polls — so "what is running" has one answer in
this codebase and not two that can disagree.

Each plan is stopped by the route that owns its kind: an execution
through ``stop_execution``, a verification through
``stop_verification``. Both are imported *inside* the function: the
route modules import ``server``, which imports this one, so a
module-level import here would be circular.

One plan's failure is one row. The others are still stopped.

The plans this call actually stopped are recorded as a *batch* (see
:func:`_write_stop_all_batch`), and the batch is the only thing
the global start will resume. Without it, a restart would pick up
every checkpoint left on disk — including the ones a previous,
unrelated stop left days ago.

get.description:
Get generated tasks with runtime status overlay + counts.

Returns ``{plan_id, tasks, counts}`` where ``tasks`` is the flat
array of task dicts (id/title/description/test_command/...) with
runtime fields overlaid from the state-machine SQLite row
(``status``, ``end_ts``, ``commit_sha``, ``attempt``,
``failure_reason``), and ``counts`` is ``{total, completed,
failed, skipped, in_progress, pending}``.

Two bugs in the previous contract are fixed:

1. **Nested-bug.** The previous implementation returned
   ``{"plan_id": ..., "tasks": <whole tasks.json>}`` — the
   whole file (which has shape ``{"tasks": [...]}``) was nested
   one level too deep, so the frontend's ``data.tasks.map(...)``
   saw a dict and crashed. The handler now extracts the array
   first (matching ``/api/execution/{plan_id}/progress``).
2. **No runtime overlay.** Without it the frontend cannot tell
   a passed task from a failed one — all tasks carried
   ``status=None`` and the task panel showed no state. We now
   overlay runtime fields from ``plan_task_repository`` (the
   same seam ``/api/execution/{plan_id}/progress`` uses).

Backward compatibility: the response still includes a ``tasks``
array — every existing field stays. Only nested-shape callers
(none in this repo) would break.

Returns:
    200 ``{"items": [...], "doc_sha256": "...", "resolved": false}``。

Raises:

get.description:
读取计划书的审核条目列表。

条目是文档的**派生视图**：5 个计划级条目（id 与顺序是契约）+ 文档里每个

``status`` / ``note`` 取自已落盘的审核状态（``verification-plan-review.
json``）。文档字节变了，那些状态一律作废（全部回到 pending）—— 旧审核
不再覆盖当前文档。

Args:
    plan_id: 计划 id。

Returns:
    200 ``{"items": [...], "doc_sha256": "..."}``。文档结构非法时条目是空
    列表（仍是 200）：条目是从合法文档里提取的，非法文档没有条目可提取 ——
    结构错误由文档端点逐条给出。

    ``doc_sha256`` 是当前计划书的字节哈希。审核者要把这一版**记下来**再
    去提交动作：文档在这期间被改过，动作端点会 409 ``document_changed``
    要求重读条目（审核不能覆盖一份已经变过的文档）。

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 ``plan_not_found``（计划目录不存在）；404
        ``document_not_found``（目录在，计划书不在）。

post.description:
Operator escape hatch — synchronously CAS a plan out of any
``verification_*`` stage (running / rerunning / repairing) into
``failed`` and persist the verification_status update.

2026-09-06:
Use this for plans that the new watchdog hasn't yet recovered
(e.g. the 12-hour-stuck ``2026-09-04 plan``
before the backend picks up the new code). Returns 200 on success
with the new stage in the response body so callers can verify the
transition before issuing follow-up requests; returns 409 if the
plan is already in an incompatible stage (already terminal, or in a
non-verification stage like ``executing``); returns 404 if the plan
does not exist in ``plan_routing``.

Side effects:
  1. ``RoutingRepository.try_mark_phase`` SQL CAS — fires
     ``KIND_PLAN_PHASE_CHANGED`` on the state bus.
  2. ``_persist_verification_terminal`` — fires ``KIND_PLAN_CLOSED``
     via ``VerificationRepository.complete_round``.
  3. Feishu notifier (already subscribed to both events) rebuilds
     the card within seconds: status flips from "still verifying"
     to "failed".

The endpoint is synchronous on purpose — operators who manually
call this for a stuck plan want to see the change in
``GET /api/plan/{id}/summary`` immediately, not after a background
task completes. The CAS itself is one SQL UPDATE so latency is
dominated by SQLite write time (sub-millisecond on local disk).

get.description:
Get VP-granularity + layer-granularity verification progress.

Returns 404 if the executor hasn't written a progress state
file yet (``verification_progress_state.json`` absent under
``plan_dir``) — the dashboard falls back to ``/status`` in that
case. Otherwise the response is the same shape whether the
in-memory ``_verification_state`` is populated or the server
was just restarted: the live state lives on disk in
``verification_progress_state.json`` (one write per
``vp_status_changed`` event), so cross-process recovery is
automatic.

Schema::

    {
      "plan_id": str,
      "verification_status": str,           # "running" | "passed" | ...
      "verification_round": int,
      "stop_reason": Optional[str],         # why the loop ended, e.g.
                                            # "max_rounds_reached" /
                                            # "same_failure_repeated_after_max_attempts"
                                            # (2026-09-19)
      "current_vp": {                       # None when no VP in flight
        "id": str,
        "title": str,
        "started_at": Optional[str]
      },
      "completed_vps": [str, ...],
      "failed_vps": [str, ...],
      "skipped_vps": [str, ...],
      "pending_vps": [str, ...],
      "current_layer": None,                # legacy field, always None
      "layer_summaries": {},                # legacy field, always empty
      "counts": {
        "total": int, "completed": int, "failed": int,
        "skipped": int, "in_progress": int, "pending": int
      },
      "last_updated_at": Optional[str]
    }

Get repair tasks generated by the verification cycle.

2026-09-11 plan v12 (cards.py repair_tasks): reads the on-disk
``plans/{id}/verification_repair_tasks.json`` snapshot first
(survives server restart), then falls back to the in-memory
``_verification_state[plan_id]["repair_tasks"]`` for the live
round's freshly generated list.

post.description:
Hard-reset a plan's verification state — direct writes, no transitions.

2026-09-17::

    "手动重启的时候，不是让状态机自动的从一个点变到另外一个点，而是
     直接去重置这个状态……只要把状态搞定了，把应该要清除掉的东西清除
     掉，它应该是一个比较固定的流程。"

Why "direct" and not the state machine: a restart is not a workflow
step, and routing it through ``transition_to`` means every restart
has to satisfy whatever transition table the current stage happens
to allow — which is where the drift the user is describing comes
from. A reset knows exactly what the state should be afterwards, so
it writes that state.

What a reset leaves behind (the "fixed procedure"):

===========================  ===============================================
``_verification_state``      in-memory entry dropped (status, results,
                             stop_reason, orchestrator, thread — all gone)
``plan_verification``        ``pending``, round ← ``restart_at_round-1``,
                             ``results``/``verdicts``/``runtime_state``/
                             ``executor_state``/``progress_state``/
                             ``execution_results`` cleared,
                             ``verification_stop_reason`` cleared
``plan_routing``             ``current_phase='verification'`` (a phase
                             ``/start`` accepts), ``current_phase``
                             mirrored, ``version`` bumped
``plan_tasks``               pending ``RP-*`` → ``voided`` (never
                             deleted: task data may only be voided or
                             created, never rewritten)

2026-10-16: the status written here was ``superseded`` and is now
``voided``. These repair rows had no work handed to breakdown
children — their *premise* (the round's verdicts) was thrown away —
so ``voided`` is the status whose resolver behaviour matches
("this will never run"), and ``superseded`` is now reserved for
"go look at my children". The request field
(``supersede_repair_tasks``) and the response key
(``cleared.superseded_repair_tasks``) deliberately keep their old
names: they are an external API contract with a test pinning them,
and renaming a response key to match an internal status word is a
breaking change for no functional gain.
``plans/<id>/`` on disk      per-round verification artifacts, when
                             ``clear_artifacts``; ``verification_plan.json``
                             only when ``clear_verification_plan``;
                             the root-cause chain's ledger and the
                             reports it names only when
                             ``clear_root_cause_chain``
===========================  ===============================================

``max_rounds`` is NOT touched — it is the plan's immutable budget
(see :class:`ResetRoundsRequest`).

Refuses with 409 while a verification thread is live: that thread
owns the orchestrator and keeps writing state, so a reset under it
would be immediately overwritten. ``force=true`` cancels the round
first and then resets.

Operator escape hatch — give the plan another batch of rounds.

Name (2026-09-16)
-----------------
Renamed from ``reset_max_rounds`` because it never touched
``max_rounds``: it resets the round **counter**. See
:class:`ResetRoundsRequest`.

Semantics (2026-09-14 — inverted from the original)
-----------------------------------------------------------------
* The plan's ``max_rounds`` is **immutable**: it is the budget the
  plan was set up with. Raising it makes rounds unbounded (the
  2026-08-25 incident: an operator lifted the cap and the counter
  together and round 6 ran for 47 minutes); lowering it silently
  rewrites the plan's setup contract. Any ``new_max_rounds`` that
  differs from the current cap is refused.
* What this endpoint DOES is reset the round **counter** — the thing
  the ``/start`` ceiling check compares against the cap. With user
  authorization the operator can hand the plan a fresh batch so the
  auto-loop iterates up to ``max_rounds`` more times.

Body::

    {}                       # restart at round 1 (default; full batch)
    {"reset_round_to": 1}    # next /start iterates rounds 1, 2, 3
    {"reset_round_to": 3}    # next /start runs round 3 only (1 left)

``reset_round_to`` is the round number the iteration **restarts at**
(1-based, the same numbering the card shows): after the cap is hit,
the counter resets to 1 and the next ``/start`` iterates from there.
It is stored internally as completed-rounds =
``value - 1`` so ``/start`` begins exactly at that round, and it may
not exceed the immutable cap (there is no round 4 of a 3-round
budget).

Side effects: the counter is written to ``plan_verification.round``
(verdicts / runtime state survive — a reset is about budget, not
about wiping progress), the row is left ``pending`` with no stop
reason, and the in-memory state is re-synced so the next ``/start``
is admitted instead of 409-ing on a stale "already running" flag.

Operator-only by convention (matches ``/start`` and ``/stop`` — no
extra auth gate). Returns
``{"plan_id", "round" (stored counter), "restart_at_round",
"rounds_remaining", "max_rounds", "new_max_rounds"}``.
Start verification via the routing/verification repositories.

get.description: Return verification status sourced from the SQLite state machine.

Liveness probe used by startup latency tests and load balancers.

2026-09-23: this answers ONLY "is the process serving HTTP".  During
the SQLite-connection outage the process was perfectly healthy by
this probe while every data endpoint returned 500, which is how the
supervisor kept reporting it "running" and the scheduler's card said
"未运行" for 40 minutes.  Whether the *data plane* works is a separate
question — see :func:`health_data_check`.

Data-plane probe: can the server actually read its state database?

Unlike :func:`health_check`, this exercises the SQLite path a real
request depends on (open + version read).  It exists because a
server can be process-healthy and data-plane-dead at the same time —
the 2026-09-23 outage had ``/health`` returning 200 while
``/api/plans`` returned 500 ``database disk image is malformed`` for
the rest of the server's life.

Deliberately read-only and cheap: it never takes the v5 migration
write lock (the fast path in ``migrate`` is a plain SELECT on a
current-schema DB).

2026-10-25: the answer also carries an ``instance`` block — the
fact sheet about the process that answered, so a reader can tell
"this instance" from "somebody else's instance on the same port"
(see :func:`_instance_identity`).  The block is purely additive:
``status``, ``plan_routing_rows`` and ``reason`` keep exactly the
meaning they had.

2026-10-26: the answer carries the guard's own verdict as
``request_guard`` — ``"enforced"`` when this process checked
itself and found the guard refusing, ``"failed"`` when the check
ran and the guard did not refuse, ``"unchecked"`` when no check
has run here (an application that was imported rather than
started).  It is the field a reader compares when the answer came
from a port they did not start themselves: an instance that
publishes ``"enforced"`` is one that proved it; one that does not
publish the field at all is somebody else.

The verdict is not the whole of the record, so the answer carries
the record too: ``request_guard_detail`` says when the check ran
(``checked_at``), which paths it asked (``paths``), and what each of
them answered with and without the header
(``status_without_header`` / ``status_with_header``).  This is the
evidence the round could not get on its own — the instance checked
**itself** before it began serving, and this is what it found.  A
round that reaches a port whose instance has since died cannot ask
the instance any more, so the record has to be published while the
instance is still there.

post.description: Generic start endpoint that returns a fresh run identifier.

get.description:
Serve one file from the frontend bundle — and nothing else.

The route exists to serve the UI's static assets (``index.html``,
``app.js``, ``style.css`` today). It is deliberately a catch-all
rather than one route per file so that adding an asset does not mean
editing the server — which is exactly why it needs an explicit
containment check rather than relying on the URL shape.
